where: Customers → open the company. The name at the top of the record.
expect_sentence: The company itself, plus its jobs and its vehicle, because the company name is stored on those too.
verify: Check the name on the customer record matches exactly, including the ZZAUTOTEST prefix.

what: The same name with every space removed
where: Customers → the company name. Nothing to set up — the old search stored a second, space-free copy of the name.
expect_sentence: The same records as the full name. People type company names without spaces and it still worked.
verify: Nothing to check on the record — this tests the search, not the data.

what: A few letters from the MIDDLE of the name
where: Customers → the company name. Taken from Br-idgepor-t.
expect_sentence: The company and everything carrying its name. Mid-word fragments matched.
verify: Nothing on the record — this tests how matching worked.
on_v2_today: Still works on the new version.

where: Customers → open the company → Address line 1.
expect_sentence: Only the customer. Nothing else is on that street.
verify: Open the company and read Address line 1 — it should say 1450 Kestrelway Industrial.

what: The SECOND line of the address
where: Customers → open the company → Address line 2.
expect_sentence: Only the customer. This line is often blank on records, which is why it is worth checking.
verify: Open the company and read Address line 2 — it should say Dock 7B. If it is empty, the test proves nothing.

where: Customers → open the company → City.
expect_sentence: TWO customers — both test companies are in Fernvale.
verify: Read the City field on both test customers.

what: A few letters from the middle of the TOWN
where: Customers → open the company → City. Taken from F-ernva-le.
expect_sentence: Both Fernvale customers. The old search treated the town exactly like the name.
verify: Nothing on the record — this tests matching.
on_v2_today: Returns NOTHING on the new version, while the same kind of fragment from the company NAME still works. Raised as SV-10060.

where: Customers → open the company → State or province. Suppliers have the same field.
expect_sentence: Both customers AND the supplier — all three are in Ohio.
verify: Read State or province on the two customers and the supplier.

where: Customers → open the company → Postal code.
expect_sentence: Only the customer with that postcode.
verify: Read Postal code on the company — it should be 44872-9931.

where: Customers → open the company → Telephone.
expect_sentence: Only the customer. Typed with dashes, which is the form the old search stored.
verify: Read Telephone on the company — (419) 555-0143. If it is blank, nothing can be proved.

what: Only PART of that phone number
where: Customers → open the company → Telephone. The last part of it.
expect_sentence: The customer. The old search looked anywhere inside the record, so part of a number was enough.
verify: Same field as above.
on_v2_today: Returns NOTHING on the new version. A person rarely has the whole number. Part of SV-10057.

where: Customers → open the company → Website.
expect_sentence: Only the customer.
verify: Read Website on the company. It is often blank on real records.

where: Customers → open the company → the Contacts list → First name.
expect_sentence: The COMPANY, not a separate contact row. A contact match returned the business they work for.
verify: Open the company, open its Contacts list, confirm Marlene Okonkwo is there.
on_v2_today: Returns 18 rows, only 2 of which contain the word. The rest are Darlene, Charlene, Martens, Marine and Alene. Raised as SV-10025.

where: Customers → open the company → Contacts → Last name.
expect_sentence: The company that person works for.
verify: Same Contacts list.

where: Customers → open the company → Contacts → Title.
expect_sentence: The company. Somebody who only remembers a job title could still find the business.
verify: Open the Contacts list and confirm the Title field reads Dispatch Supervisor. It is frequently empty.
on_v2_today: Reported as returning nothing. Open for the product owner.

where: Customers → open the company → Contacts → Telephone. Different from the company's number.
expect_sentence: The company. Note this is the CONTACT's number, not the switchboard.
verify: Confirm the contact's own Telephone is set and differs from the company's.

where: Assets → open the vehicle → Unit. Shops label their own trucks with these.
expect_sentence: Only the vehicle.
verify: Read Unit on the vehicle record.

where: Assets → open the vehicle → VIN / Serial number.
expect_sentence: Only the vehicle.
verify: Read the VIN field, all 17 characters.
on_v2_today: Still works on the new version.

what: Only the LAST PART of that chassis number
where: Assets → the same VIN field, last six characters.
expect_sentence: The vehicle. This is how somebody reads a number off a windscreen.
verify: Same VIN field — check the last characters match what you type.
on_v2_today: Returns NOTHING on the new version. Raised as SV-10058.

where: Assets → open the vehicle → Licence plate.
expect_sentence: Only the vehicle.
verify: Read Licence plate on the vehicle. Often blank on real records.

where: Assets → open the vehicle → Year. It is also the first thing in the vehicle's displayed name.
expect_sentence: The vehicle. On a real shop's data this would return many.
verify: Read Year on the vehicle.

where: Assets → open the vehicle → Make.
expect_sentence: The vehicle.
verify: Read Make on the vehicle.

where: Assets → open the vehicle → Model.
expect_sentence: The vehicle.
verify: Read Model on the vehicle.

what: The year AND the make together
where: Assets → the vehicle's displayed name is year, make, then model — so this is the start of it.
expect_sentence: The vehicle. It matched because the displayed name STARTS with what you typed.
verify: Check the vehicle shows as 2019 Freightliner Cascadia.
on_v2_today: Returns NO vehicles at all. Raised as SV-10055.

what: The job number with nothing in front
where: Work orders → the Number column, with the letter, dash and shop number stripped off.
expect_sentence: The job. People read the digits off a printed sheet and type only those.
verify: Open the job and read its number.

what: The job number as it is written
where: Work orders → the Number column, as displayed.
expect_sentence: The job.
verify: Read the number on the job.

what: The job number with the SHOP number in front
where: Work orders → the Number column. Different shops write it differently, so the old search stored four forms.
expect_sentence: The job. All four written forms matched.
verify: Compare the number on screen with the shop number on the branch.

where: Work orders → the Status column, or the status on the job itself.
expect_sentence: Every job in that status — this is how a dispatcher pulled up all the estimates at once.
verify: Read the Status on the job.
on_v2_today: Reported as returning no jobs. Open for the product owner.

what: A TWO-WORD status typed as one word
where: Work orders → the Status column, for a status like Quality check.
expect_sentence: The job in that status. The old search deliberately joined the words.
verify: Find a job whose status is Quality check.

where: Parts → Vendors → open the supplier. The name at the top.
expect_sentence: Only the supplier.
verify: Read the name on the supplier record.

where: Parts → Vendors → open the supplier → Address line 1.
expect_sentence: Only the supplier.
verify: Read Address line 1 on the supplier.

where: Parts → Vendors → open the supplier → Address line 2.
expect_sentence: Only the supplier. Worth checking because this field is usually empty.
verify: Read Address line 2 on the supplier. If blank, the test proves nothing.

where: Parts → Vendors → open the supplier → City.
expect_sentence: Only the supplier.
verify: Read City on the supplier.

where: Parts → Vendors → open the supplier → Postal code.
expect_sentence: Only the supplier.
verify: Read Postal code on the supplier.

where: Parts → Vendors → open the supplier → Telephone.
expect_sentence: Only the supplier.
verify: Read Telephone on the supplier.

where: Parts → Vendors → open the supplier → Email.
expect_sentence: Only the supplier. Note customers have no email of their own — only their contacts do.
verify: Read Email on the supplier.

where: Parts → Parts catalogue → open the part → Part number.
expect_sentence: The part. This one has NEVER been stocked, which is the point of it.
verify: Open the catalogue part and read its number.

what: The part number with the DASHES removed
where: Parts → the same Part number field. The old search stored a dash-free copy as well.
expect_sentence: The same part. Nobody types the dashes.
verify: Nothing on the record — this tests the search.

what: A word from the part's DESCRIPTION
where: Parts → Parts catalogue → open the part → the description or name.
expect_sentence: The part — and this is the important one. The old search read the CATALOGUE, so a part the shop has never held was still findable.
verify: Confirm the part exists in the catalogue and has NO stock. That absence is the test.
on_v2_today: Reported as not findable at all. The strongest finding of the batch.

what: A name ONE letter away from a real one
where: Customers → there are two test companies, one with Marlene and one with Darlene, created one letter apart on purpose.
expect_sentence: ONLY the Darlene company. The old search never offered you a different spelling from the one you typed.
verify: Check both companies exist so the pair is meaningful.
on_v2_today: Typing Marlene on the new version returns the Darlene records too. That is SV-10025.

where: Nothing to set up.
expect_sentence: NOTHING is matched. Your recently opened records are shown instead. The old search waited for two characters.
verify: Nothing to check.

where: Nothing to set up.
expect_sentence: No match — so your recently opened records come back, leaving you something to click.
verify: Nothing to check.
